en: Whatever Kumayyk bites,
It will utterly destroy.
Kumayyk, the good fortune you encountered—
Would it shrink from a tiger?
When this Kumayyk grows,
Would it recoil from anything?
Its lion-like nature is complete.
This creature Kumayyk—
Will it not do as it pleases,
And wolves, whole packs of them,
Slaughter before your eyes?
Upon the person rearing it,
They said, distress will fall;
Beyond the fanged beasts,
They said, an enemy will fall upon them.
Kumayyk will be a precious creature.
If it spends three days in the wild,
They said, the unseen will rear it.
No male human must come near;
The purest of women,
A wife, they said, must rear it.
And among those women,
One skilled with spear and bow,
They said, must rear it capably.
One who knows the enemy's devices thoroughly,
An outstanding woman, they said, must rear it.
The woman who rears Kumayyk—
Consider what her courage must be!
She will have no rest by day;
The soul who rears Kumayyk
Will have no sleep at night.
Until six full months have passed,
The ordeal of Judgment Day,
They said, she will suffer terribly.
A wondrous, generous-hearted woman,
They said, must rear it capably;
What will happen six months hence,
One who knows it clearly and thoroughly,
An outstanding woman, they said, must rear it.
This blessed Kumayyk,
Unless it is reared in that way,
One day its desire
It will attain, they said.
When one looks, unseen by the eye,
With no knowing where it is,
If a man rears it, one day,
They said, it will go away.
If you marry Kanykey, Khan Manas,
You will enter blessed good fortune, he says.
How to rear Kumayyk—
Kanykey, Karakan's daughter,
That poor soul will know, he says.
Oh, my child Manas, hear my words:
Fond of bed, easy upon her husband,
The wife you married, Akylay,
That ill-mannered, slack and flighty woman,
Oh, that frivolous unbeliever,
Akylay, Shooruk's daughter,
Oh, that rustling, flighty unbeliever!
Utterly foolish, abrupt in temper,
Oh, that hot-tempered, unruly unbeliever!
My companion's wife Akylay,
Oh, that ill-mannered unbeliever,
One day its desire
It will attain, they said.
Your strikingly lovely unbeliever,
With gossip multiplying, jealousy burning,
My bloodthirsty one, do not fall into trouble.
Unless you die, Manas, you will see:
Your Bakay will intervene.
If you rely on your own judgment,
What you have gained will go to waste.
If you stay with Akylay,
Know now what I am saying:
From your court will flee
Your mullah who reads the lessons;
Your companion will flee your host.
“Khan Manas's Akylay
Is a hot-tempered troublemaker,” they will say,
“Will she curse us?” they will say.
Your people will flee your home;
Not one of your affairs will prosper.
Your wife who knows no custom—
Where did that unbeliever come from?
You have thought, “I have a wife,”
But, my bloodthirsty Manas, you are a bachelor!
What Akylay is like,
I shall tell you, Manas; understand,
Lion Manas, heed my words.
Her speech is shrill and coarse;
There are signs she will bear no child.
The forty companions from forty places,
If they speak delightful, precious words,
She shows her rudeness.
Think for yourself, Manas:
Of the forty champions, Akylay—
Which one will she let into the house?
While this Akylay remains,
This Talas will be no homeland for you;
The forty warriors will be no people for you.
Your head will fall into worry.
While Akylay is there,
The forty warriors will wander away.
This wife of yours, Akylay,
Your frenzied, mad unbeliever,
Will not join what has broken,
Will not gather what has scattered.
While this Akylay remains,
Will your one self become two?
Drawing close beside you,
Will the forty warriors pitch their camp?
A warrior's torn
Coat of armor—will she mend and patch it?
Finding their occasion to take offense,
Saying, “Your wife is wicked,”
Will not your forty warriors stir up trouble?
I pieced it together from tradition;
I asked those who know.
Karakan, the khan of Bukhara,
Is a man of sacred powers, they said.
One son, many daughters—
He has twelve daughters, they said.
That khan's twelve daughters
Are wives for twelve khans, they said.
The deftest with a brass thimble,
The finest among so many,
The firstborn, the eldest daughter,
The beauty among his daughters,
Akerkech, whom hero Kökchö married,
Is also his daughter, they say.
His daughters are all blessed good fortune;
Consider this, Manas, and understand.
The youngest of the twelve daughters,
A servant beloved of God,
A dark-complexioned beauty,
A radiant one among Muslims,
The purest of the long-haired,
A sovereign among women,
Her utterances are like gold;
Her speech is a plea to Allah, they said.
Six months ahead, the coming
Death and suffering,
Arrivals and departures,
She can tell without delay.
That poor soul, unlike other humans,
Has sacred powers, they said.
Marry Kanykey and you will prosper;
You will be sovereign over the people.
If Kanykey comes to Talas,
Blessed good fortune will cross your path.
If you live safely, you will see:
While Kanykey is there,
Those who fled will return to your host.
She will make your concerns numberless;
Your vast treasury of riches,
As soon as she comes, she will fill.
Lend your ear to my words:
Kanykey, Karakan's daughter,
Take her as your bride.
That unbeliever Kanykey
Has wisdom unlike other humans'.
Your self, weighty as a mountain,
By planting she will make a garden,
By building she will make a house;
Your illustrious self
She will make khan over the earth.
If you marry Kanykey, leopard,
Your wretched, hard-stepping horse
She will rear into a wondrous steed;
She will promptly do you service!
Your tigress of a hero,
Your fairy-born unbeliever—
If you marry Kanykey, my Manas,
Your khanship will be famed among the people;
Your single self will become a thousand!
Its stride will stretch across the world,
Your tireless racer like Akkula;
With joyful cries they will camp beside you,
Your other kinsmen who had strayed!
If you marry Kanykey,
She will be a queen to you.
“Leopard Bakay found her,” you must say,
And be grateful to me!
She will put the treasury's riches safely away;
She will exalt your khanship.
Such is Kanykey's nature.
A wise one among women—
No such one is born
Among wives in white headscarves!
When you marry her, your affairs will prosper.
Try that fierce woman in every way;
She will move and settle with white yurts.
Bind her betrothal, become in-laws—
Would she be a wife who merely flatters?
Kanykey, the finest of brides,
Will gather your treasures, leaving nothing lacking.
That graceful, ill-fated woman—
If she survives, you will see—
Will lift your burden for you!
“If only my wolf-maned one lives,”
Dear, poor Kanykey
Would think, even if her head were severed.
However many hardships fell upon her,
She would never once show distress.
A noble among women,
If you marry Kanykey,
She will be mother to the forty warriors,
The most capable among women,
The finest of the white-headscarved.
This is what I say; understand,
My lion Manas, heed my words!
That she will be Manas's wife,
Does she not come already knowing?
A close-fitting garment no bullet can pierce,
Does she not come wearing?
Upon anyone who provokes her, great strife—
Does she not come bringing it?
Chong Ayar, who lifts a camel—
Does she not come bringing him?
When he comes in fury,
His fierce rage begins;
When his fierce rage comes,
He throws a punch at a camel and misses.
In keeping with your earlier words,
She will grant Ayar as a lasting gift
And make him a warrior for you.
Becoming in-laws, driving livestock,
Bowing in homage, chewing fat—
Unless we go and bow in homage,
Unless we agree to her words,
Unless Kumayyk, into her hands,
We place as a trust—
That gracious Kanykey
Will hang an amulet about its neck;
She is the one to rear Kumayyk.
One whose words it will obey,
That puppy Kumayyk
She will rear properly for you.
If you pay no heed to my words,
If you do not take this advice,
To the ancient city of Bukhara,
While Kanykey is there,
No one can endure going.
Does any mortal dare face her?
That poor soul Kanykey—
Can a human defeat her face to face?
Would she shrink from battle?
Would a human return without being slaughtered?
She is deft with the spear, they say,
A sage of exceptional wisdom,
A merciless champion, they say.
Hearing news of the fierce woman,
The Kazakhs went to besiege her, they say.
Saying, “I shall take the fierce woman,”
All the mighty giants
Went together to besiege her, they say.
